text.en: Raju saw an earthworm, a fish and a sparrow on one day. "How do scientists sort so many animals?" he asked.

Classification is the arrangement of organisms into groups on the basis of similarities, differences and relationships. Taxonomy is the science of classification. In the classification used here, the main ranks range from kingdom down to species. A modern system can also place domains above kingdoms. The scientific name of a species has two parts: a capitalised genus name and a lowercase specific name. When typed, both parts are generally italicised.
Animals are grouped by features such as germ layers. Animals with two germ layers, the ectoderm and the endoderm, are diploblastic, and those with three layers (ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm) are triploblastic. A chordate has a notochord at some stage of development. Vertebrates are chordates with a backbone. Some other chordates have no backbone.
Invertebrate phyla include sponges, coelenterates, flatworms, roundworms, segmented worms like earthworms and leeches, arthropods with jointed legs, molluscs and the spiny-skinned animals such as starfish. Arthropoda is the largest phylum, and its members cast off and regrow their exoskeleton, which is moulting. Chordates include fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

Invertebrate phyla include sponges, coelenterates, flatworms, roundworms, segmented worms like earthworms and leeches, arthropods with jointed legs, molluscs and the spiny-skinned animals such as starfish.
A field guide might group animals by shared body features. Modern classification also considers evidence about relationships. Similar features can give a starting clue.
Read the main ranks in order from broad to narrow. An animal belongs to a kingdom, a phylum, a class, an order, a family, a genus and a species.

board.text: Kingdom → phylum → class → order → family → genus → species

text.en: In the name Homo sapiens, Homo is the genus. Its first letter is capitalised. Sapiens is written in lowercase within the scientific name.
A body with bilateral symmetry can be divided into matching left and right sides by a suitable plane. A butterfly viewed from above is a familiar model.
An animal with radial symmetry has repeated structures around a central axis. Several planes through that axis can divide a suitable example into matching parts.

board.text: Radial: pattern around a central axis

text.en: Germ layers are layers of cells in an early embryo. They contribute to tissues as the animal develops. The two-layer and three-layer terms describe that early organisation.
A true coelom is a fluid-filled body cavity lined with tissue from the mesoderm. Flatworms lack a coelom. Roundworms have a cavity that is not completely lined that way.

board.text: Compare how the body cavity is lined

text.en: Sponges have numerous pores and channels. Water moves through them, and the animal can obtain food particles from that water. Sponges do not have true tissues like those in other animals.
Cnidarians include corals and jellyfish. They have distinctive stinging cells and often show radial symmetry. These features help distinguish them from sponges.
A flatworm has a flattened body. Roundworms have a more cylindrical shape and are not divided into repeated segments like an earthworm.

board.text: Flatworms vs roundworms: compare body shapes

text.en: An earthworm has repeated segments along its elongated body. Segmentation is an important clue for annelids. Leeches are another annelid example.
An arthropod has jointed appendages and an external skeleton. Insects and crustaceans are examples. Growth can involve shedding the old external skeleton in a process called moulting.
Molluscs have soft bodies and often have a muscular foot or a modification of it. Some have shells. Snails and octopuses show how different members of one phylum can appear.
Adult sea stars have a radial body pattern and use tube feet. They belong to Echinodermata, a group of marine animals that also includes sea urchins.

board.text: Echinoderms: marine animals with tube feet

text.en: Acorn worms are hemichordates. The name resembles chordate, but hemichordates are a separate phylum. A similar name alone is not enough to establish group membership.
Chordate features include a notochord and a dorsal hollow nerve cord at some stage of development. A tunicate larva illustrates that an animal can be a chordate without a backbone.

board.text: Notochord is different from a backbone

text.en: Fishes generally use gills and have fins that help them move. Sharks have mainly cartilaginous skeletons, whereas many familiar fishes have mainly bony skeletons.

board.text: Compare cartilage and bone in fishes

text.en: Amphibians often show different body forms over their life cycle. For example, a frog tadpole and an adult frog differ in their structures and how they move.
Reptiles such as lizards have dry scales. Birds have feathers. Their distinguishing features help place familiar examples within the vertebrates.

board.text: Reptile example: dry scales · bird: feathers

text.en: Mammals have hair at some stage and produce milk for their young. Bats and whales are mammals, although their movements and habitats differ greatly.
Sort a snail, a crab and a fish by first comparing body features. Look for a soft body and foot, jointed limbs, or a backbone. Each clue supports a different grouping.
When you finish a classification, cite the feature that supports your choice. A whale and a fish both swim, but their features and relationships put them in different groups.

board.text: Explain both the group and the supporting feature

problem.en: A whale and a fish both swim in water. Which evidence distinguishes the mammal from the fish?

text.en: Compare characteristic features beyond swimming.

why.en: A whale breathes air with lungs and nurses its young with milk.

text.en: Classify the whale as a mammal.

why.en: Fish generally use gills, and milk production is a defining mammal feature.

prompt.en: A friend says Chordates are animals without a backbone. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: Chordates have a notochord or backbone.

points.en: Taxonomy is the science of classification.
The species is the lowest category.
Chordates have a notochord at some stage. Vertebrates are the chordates with backbones.
